CRIME VICTIM AND DOMESTIC VIOLENCE LEAVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet is provided by Acme, Inc. to Jordan Lee to explain, on a general informational basis only, California's job-protected leave and anti-retaliation protections for an employee who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or certain other crimes -- or who has a family member who is such a victim -- when taking time off from work for reasons connected to that victimization, such as obtaining a restraining order, seeking medical or psychological treatment, attending related court proceedings, or engaging in safety planning. It states general facts about how California law in this area works, including how that law has changed over time and where it is presently codified. It does not describe Jordan Lee's own situation, does not determine whether Jordan Lee or any other person qualifies as a victim or a family member of a victim under any statute, and does not advise Jordan Lee or Acme, Inc. on what to do about any actual circumstance.

WHERE THIS PROTECTION IS CODIFIED TODAY
California Labor Code §§ 230 and 230.1 were, for many years, the primary statutes protecting an employee who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or certain other crimes -- including the additional leave purposes those sections made available to employees of larger employers. Both sections remain on the books, but by their own current terms each now applies only to alleged actions or inactions occurring on or before December 31, 2024, and each is scheduled for repeal on January 1, 2035. Effective January 1, 2025, this same body of protection was relocated into the Fair Employment and Housing Act, and is presently codified at Government Code § 12945.8, most recently amended by AB 406 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 148), effective October 1, 2025. This information sheet accordingly describes the substance of the former Labor Code §§ 230 and 230.1 protections, and separately identifies where that same protection is now found and how its scope has changed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(k) This section shall apply only to alleged actions or inactions occurring on or before December 31, 2024. (l) This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2035, and as of that date is repealed."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230(k)-(l), transitional applicability limit and scheduled repeal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.)
  "(i) This section shall apply only to alleged actions or inactions occurring on or before December 31, 2024. (j) This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2035, and as of that date is repealed."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.1 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.1(i)-(j), transitional applicability limit and scheduled repeal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.1.)
  "(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 148, Sec. 1. (AB 406) Effective October 1, 2025.)"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8, amendment history note (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  Known gap: This section's independent verification of Labor Code § 230.1's current transitional status is a genuine extension beyond this corpus's existing Jury Duty and Witness Leave Information Sheet, which addressed only the jury-duty and witness-leave portions of former Labor Code § 230 and expressly declined to make any claim about § 230.1's current status. This document does not address whether any particular employee's leave, taken before or after any of these transition dates, is governed by the former or the current statute, and it does not independently verify secondary commentary about the legislative history of AB 2499 or AB 406 -- only the current statutory text of Labor Code §§ 230 and 230.1 and Government Code § 12945.8 was verified. The Labor Code § 230 citation and the Labor Code § 230.1 citation below are each drawn from a single subsection of their respective, separately-numbered sections, so the two Labor Code citations are independent of each other; the Government Code citation is from a third, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

CORE VICTIM LEAVE PROTECTION AND JOB PROTECTION
Under former Labor Code § 230(c) -- and, for present-day conduct, under Government Code § 12945.8(a)(3) -- an employer may not discharge an employee, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee, who is a victim for taking time off from work to obtain or attempt to obtain relief such as a temporary restraining order, restraining order, or other injunctive relief intended to help ensure the health, safety, or welfare of the victim or the victim's child. Government Code § 12945.8(a)(4) separately prohibits, commencing January 1, 2026, discharge or discrimination or retaliation against an employee who is a victim or a family member of a victim for taking time off to attend judicial proceedings related to the crime, including a delinquency proceeding, a postarrest release decision, a plea, a sentencing, a postconviction release decision, or any proceeding in which a right of that person is at issue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(3) Discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim for taking time off from work to obtain or attempt to obtain any relief. Relief includes, but is not limited to, a temporary restraining order, restraining order, or other injunctive relief, to help ensure the health, safety, or welfare of the victim or their child."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(3), victim relief leave protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(4) Commencing January 1, 2026, discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim or a family member of a victim for taking time off from work in order to attend judicial proceedings related to that crime, including, but not limited to, any delinquency proceeding, a postarrest release decision, plea, sentencing, postconviction release decision, or any proceeding where a right of that person is an issue."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(4), judicial-proceeding leave (commencing January 1, 2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(c) An employer shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim for taking time off from work to obtain or attempt to obtain any relief. Relief includes, but is not limited to, a temporary restraining order, restraining order, or other injunctive relief, to help ensure the health, safety, or welfare of the victim or their child."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230(c), the historical version of the same victim relief leave protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.)
  Known gap: This clause does not restate the separate witness-leave protection already covered by this corpus's existing Jury Duty and Witness Leave Information Sheet (Government Code § 12945.8(a)(2), extended to but not limited to victims). It also does not resolve who qualifies as a 'victim' or 'family member' for these purposes -- those are defined terms addressed only in general terms elsewhere in this document -- nor does it address the January 1, 2026 commencement date of subdivision (a)(4) in relation to any particular set of facts. The Government Code § 12945.8(a)(3) and § 12945.8(a)(4) citations below are two paragraphs of the same subdivision of the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(c) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

ADDITIONAL LEAVE PURPOSES FOR EMPLOYERS WITH 25 OR MORE EMPLOYEES
Former Labor Code § 230.1(a), and now Government Code § 12945.8(b), each impose an additional, broader set of job-protection duties that apply only to an employer with 25 or more employees. Under the current Government Code § 12945.8(b), such an employer may not discharge, discriminate, or retaliate against an employee who is a victim, or who has a family member who is a victim, for taking time off from work for any of ten enumerated purposes, including seeking relief for a family member, seeking or assisting a family member to seek medical attention, domestic-violence-shelter or victim services, or psychological counseling, participating in safety planning, relocating, providing care to a recovering family member, seeking legal services, attending legal proceedings, or arranging childcare or dependent care made necessary by the qualifying act of violence. The former Labor Code § 230.1(a) covered a narrower set of four purposes for the same 25-or-more-employee threshold: seeking medical attention, obtaining domestic-violence-shelter or victim services, obtaining psychological counseling, and safety planning or relocation. Government Code § 12945.8(i) also allows an employer to cap total leave taken for these subdivision (b) purposes at 12 weeks, and to impose a shorter 5-day or 10-day cap in certain circumstances where the leave is taken because of a family member's (rather than the employee's own) victimization.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(b) An employer with 25 or more employees shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim or who has a family member who is a victim for taking time off from work for any of the following purposes:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(b), the 25-or-more-employee threshold for expanded leave purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(1) An employer may limit total leave time taken pursuant to subdivision (b) to 12 weeks. (2) If an employee’s family member is a victim who is not deceased as a result of a crime, and the employee is not a victim, and the employee takes leave pursuant to paragraph (6) of subdivision (b), the employer may limit the leave taken for that reason to five days. (3) If any employee’s family member is a victim who is not deceased as a result of crime, and the employee is not a victim, the employer may limit the total leave taken pursuant to subdivision (b) to 10 days."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(i)(1)-(3), caps an employer may place on subdivision (b) leave (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(a) In addition to the requirements and prohibitions imposed on employees pursuant to Section 230, an employer with 25 or more employees shall not discharge, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against, an employee who is a victim, for taking time off from work for any of the following purposes: (1) To seek medical attention for injuries caused by crime or abuse. (2) To obtain services from a domestic violence shelter, program, rape crisis center, or victim services organization or agency as a result of the crime or abuse. (3) To obtain psychological counseling or mental health services related to an experience of crime or abuse. (4) To participate in safety planning and take other actions to increase safety from future crime or abuse, including temporary or permanent relocation."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230.1 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230.1(a), the historical four-purpose version of the 25-or-more-employee leave, same employer-size threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.1.)
  Known gap: This clause states the 25-or-more-employee threshold and the numbers and general subject matter of the enumerated purposes as they appear in the statutory text; it does not attempt to state which specific facts satisfy any one of those purposes, and it does not address how an employer's total employee count is measured or on what date it is measured, none of which the text of either section specifies. It also does not restate the corpus's existing citation to Government Code § 12945.8(b)'s chapeau language, but independently re-verifies it here. The two Government Code § 12945.8 citations below (the subdivision (b) chapeau and the leave-cap subdivision (i)) are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230.1(a) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both -- it is this independent Labor Code source that establishes the historical, narrower four-purpose list, in contrast to the current ten-purpose list.

ADVANCE NOTICE AND CERTIFICATION
As a condition of taking time off for the relief-leave, family-relief, or 25-or-more-employee purposes described above, Government Code § 12945.8(c)(1) states that the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee's intention to take time off, unless advance notice is not feasible. When an unscheduled absence occurs instead, § 12945.8(c)(2) provides that the employer shall not take action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification -- which the statute treats as sufficient in several listed forms, including a police report, a qualifying court order or other court or prosecutorial evidence of a court appearance, documentation from a licensed medical professional, domestic violence counselor, sexual assault counselor, victim advocate, or other health care provider or counselor, or another form of documentation that reasonably verifies the qualifying act of violence occurred. Former Labor Code § 230(d)(2) contained a substantively similar certification list.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(c) (1) As a condition of taking time off for a purpose set forth in paragraph (1), (3), or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b), the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee’s intention to take time off, unless the advance notice is not feasible."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(1), advance notice condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(2) When an unscheduled absence occurs, the employer shall not take any action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification to the employer upon request by the employer. Certification shall be sufficient in the form of any of the following: (A) A police report indicating that the employee or a family member of the employee was a victim."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(2), certification after an unscheduled absence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(2) When an unscheduled absence occurs, the employer shall not take any action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification to the employer. Certification shall be sufficient in the form of any of the following: (A) A police report indicating that the employee was a victim."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230(d)(2), the historical version of the same certification provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.)
  Known gap: This clause does not attempt to define how much advance notice is 'reasonable' or when advance notice is 'not feasible,' terms the statute does not itself define. It also does not restate the full text of every certification category, only the general structure and some examples, and it does not address the reasonable-accommodation-specific certification and recertification provisions found elsewhere in § 12945.8(e)(7), which this document treats separately. The two Government Code § 12945.8 citations below (subdivisions (c)(1) and (c)(2)) are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(d)(2) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

CONFIDENTIALITY OF LEAVE AND ACCOMMODATION RECORDS
Government Code § 12945.8(c)(3) states that, to the extent allowed by law, an employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under the relief-leave, judicial-proceeding, or 25-or-more-employee provisions, and that furnishing evidence or a certification does not waive any confidentiality or privilege that may otherwise exist between the employee or the employee's family member and a third party. A parallel confidentiality duty applies to reasonable-accommodation documentation under § 12945.8(e)(7)(D): any verbal or written statement, police or court record, or other documentation identifying an employee or the employee's family member as a victim must be maintained as confidential by the employer and not disclosed except as required by federal or state law or as necessary to protect the employee's safety in the workplace, and the employee must be given notice before any authorized disclosure. Former Labor Code § 230(d)(3) contained the same confidentiality duty for relief-leave requests.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(3) To the extent allowed by law and consistent with subparagraph (D) of paragraph (7) of subdivision (e), the employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under paragraph (3) or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b). Furnishing evidence or providing a certification under this subdivision shall not waive any confidentiality or privilege that may exist between the employee or employee’s family member and a third party."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(3), confidentiality of a leave request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(D) Any verbal or written statement, police or court record, or other documentation provided to an employer identifying an employee or the employee’s family member as a victim shall be maintained as confidential by the employer and shall not be disclosed by the employer except as required by federal or state law or as necessary to protect the employee’s safety in the workplace. The employee shall be given notice before any authorized disclosure."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(e)(7)(D), confidentiality of accommodation-related documentation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(3) To the extent allowed by law and consistent with subparagraph (D) of paragraph (7) of subdivision (f), the employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under subdivision (c)."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230(d)(3), the historical version of the same confidentiality duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.)
  Known gap: This clause does not attempt to define the outer limits of 'to the extent allowed by law,' a qualifier the statute leaves undefined, and it does not address what remedy, if any, is available to an employee for a breach of this confidentiality duty -- that is not stated in the confidentiality subdivisions themselves. It also does not independently verify whether any other statute (for example, general personnel-file or privacy statutes) supplies additional confidentiality protection. The Government Code § 12945.8(c)(3) and § 12945.8(e)(7)(D) citations below are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(d)(3) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

REASONABLE ACCOMMODATION FOR WORKPLACE SAFETY
Separately from the leave provisions above, Government Code § 12945.8(e)(1) requires an employer to provide reasonable accommodations for an employee who is a victim, or whose family member is a victim, of a qualifying act of violence, when the employee requests an accommodation for the employee's safety while at work. Unlike the additional leave purposes discussed above, this accommodation duty is not limited to employers with 25 or more employees. Section 12945.8(e)(2) gives examples of reasonable accommodations, including a transfer, reassignment, modified schedule, changed work telephone or permission to carry a telephone at work, changed work station, installed lock, assistance documenting an incident, an implemented safety procedure, another adjustment to a job structure, workplace facility, or work requirement, or referral to a victim assistance organization. Section 12945.8(f) separately makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or attempt to exercise, any right provided under the section. Former Labor Code § 230(f)(1) contained a substantively similar reasonable-accommodation duty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(1) An employer shall provide reasonable accommodations for an employee who is a victim or whose family member is a victim of a qualifying act of violence who requests an accommodation for the safety of the employee while at work."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(e)(1), reasonable accommodation duty (no employer-size limit stated) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(2) For purposes of this subdivision, reasonable accommodations may include the implementation of safety measures, including a transfer, reassignment, modified schedule, changed work telephone, permission to carry telephone at work, changed work station, installed lock, assistance in documenting domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or another qualifying act of violence that occurs in the workplace, an implemented safety procedure, or another adjustment to a job structure, workplace facility, or work requirement in response to domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or other qualifying act of violence, or referral to a victim assistance organization."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(e)(2), examples of reasonable accommodations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(f) It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(f), general anti-interference provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(1) An employer shall provide reasonable accommodations for a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, who requests an accommodation for the safety of the victim while at work."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230(f)(1), the historical version of the same reasonable-accommodation duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.)
  Known gap: This clause does not attempt to define 'undue hardship,' a limit on the accommodation duty that the statute defines by cross-reference to Government Code § 12926 and Labor Code § 6400, both of which this document did not independently fetch or verify. It also does not restate the accommodation-specific certification and six-month recertification provisions found in § 12945.8(e)(7), addressing only the confidentiality portion of that paragraph in a separate clause. The Government Code § 12945.8(e)(1), § 12945.8(e)(2), and § 12945.8(f) citations below are all from the same section and are not independent of one another; the Labor Code § 230(f)(1) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of all three.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge receipt of this information sheet.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: September 1, 2026

Provided on behalf of Acme, Inc. by: _______________________________________________
Date: _______________
City/State: Oakland, California

(2) If an employee’s family member is a victim who is not deceased as a result of a crime, and the employee is not a victim, and the employee takes leave pursuant to paragraph (6) of subdivision (b), the employer may limit the leave taken for that reason to five days. (3) If any employee’s family member is a victim who is not deceased as a result of crime, and the employee is not a victim, the employer may limit the total leave taken pursuant to subdivision (b) to 10 days.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.1(a), the historical four-purpose version of the 25-or-more-employee leave, same employer-size threshold
citations.quote: (a) In addition to the requirements and prohibitions imposed on employees pursuant to Section 230, an employer with 25 or more employees shall not discharge, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against, an employee who is a victim, for taking time off from work for any of the following purposes: (1) To seek medical attention for injuries caused by crime or abuse. (2) To obtain services from a domestic violence shelter, program, rape crisis center, or victim services organization or agency as a result of the crime or abuse. (3) To obtain psychological counseling or mental health services related to an experience of crime or abuse. (4) To participate in safety planning and take other actions to increase safety from future crime or abuse, including temporary or permanent relocation.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the 25-or-more-employee threshold and the numbers and general subject matter of the enumerated purposes as they appear in the statutory text; it does not attempt to state which specific facts satisfy any one of those purposes, and it does not address how an employer's total employee count is measured or on what date it is measured, none of which the text of either section specifies. It also does not restate the corpus's existing citation to Government Code § 12945.8(b)'s chapeau language, but independently re-verifies it here. The two Government Code § 12945.8 citations below (the subdivision (b) chapeau and the leave-cap subdivision (i)) are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230.1(a) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both -- it is this independent Labor Code source that establishes the historical, narrower four-purpose list, in contrast to the current ten-purpose list.

expectedJSON.body: As a condition of taking time off for the relief-leave, family-relief, or 25-or-more-employee purposes described above, Government Code § 12945.8(c)(1) states that the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee's intention to take time off, unless advance notice is not feasible. When an unscheduled absence occurs instead, § 12945.8(c)(2) provides that the employer shall not take action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification -- which the statute treats as sufficient in several listed forms, including a police report, a qualifying court order or other court or prosecutorial evidence of a court appearance, documentation from a licensed medical professional, domestic violence counselor, sexual assault counselor, victim advocate, or other health care provider or counselor, or another form of documentation that reasonably verifies the qualifying act of violence occurred. Former Labor Code § 230(d)(2) contained a substantively similar certification list.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(1), advance notice condition
citations.quote: (c) (1) As a condition of taking time off for a purpose set forth in paragraph (1), (3), or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b), the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee’s intention to take time off, unless the advance notice is not feasible.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(2), certification after an unscheduled absence
citations.quote: (2) When an unscheduled absence occurs, the employer shall not take any action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification to the employer upon request by the employer. Certification shall be sufficient in the form of any of the following: (A) A police report indicating that the employee or a family member of the employee was a victim.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230(d)(2), the historical version of the same certification provision
citations.quote: (2) When an unscheduled absence occurs, the employer shall not take any action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification to the employer. Certification shall be sufficient in the form of any of the following: (A) A police report indicating that the employee was a victim.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not attempt to define how much advance notice is 'reasonable' or when advance notice is 'not feasible,' terms the statute does not itself define. It also does not restate the full text of every certification category, only the general structure and some examples, and it does not address the reasonable-accommodation-specific certification and recertification provisions found elsewhere in § 12945.8(e)(7), which this document treats separately. The two Government Code § 12945.8 citations below (subdivisions (c)(1) and (c)(2)) are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(d)(2) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

expectedJSON.body: Government Code § 12945.8(c)(3) states that, to the extent allowed by law, an employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under the relief-leave, judicial-proceeding, or 25-or-more-employee provisions, and that furnishing evidence or a certification does not waive any confidentiality or privilege that may otherwise exist between the employee or the employee's family member and a third party. A parallel confidentiality duty applies to reasonable-accommodation documentation under § 12945.8(e)(7)(D): any verbal or written statement, police or court record, or other documentation identifying an employee or the employee's family member as a victim must be maintained as confidential by the employer and not disclosed except as required by federal or state law or as necessary to protect the employee's safety in the workplace, and the employee must be given notice before any authorized disclosure. Former Labor Code § 230(d)(3) contained the same confidentiality duty for relief-leave requests.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(3), confidentiality of a leave request
citations.quote: (3) To the extent allowed by law and consistent with subparagraph (D) of paragraph (7) of subdivision (e), the employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under paragraph (3) or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b). Furnishing evidence or providing a certification under this subdivision shall not waive any confidentiality or privilege that may exist between the employee or employee’s family member and a third party.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(e)(7)(D), confidentiality of accommodation-related documentation
citations.quote: (D) Any verbal or written statement, police or court record, or other documentation provided to an employer identifying an employee or the employee’s family member as a victim shall be maintained as confidential by the employer and shall not be disclosed by the employer except as required by federal or state law or as necessary to protect the employee’s safety in the workplace. The employee shall be given notice before any authorized disclosure.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230(d)(3), the historical version of the same confidentiality duty
citations.quote: (3) To the extent allowed by law and consistent with subparagraph (D) of paragraph (7) of subdivision (f), the employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under subdivision (c).

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not attempt to define the outer limits of 'to the extent allowed by law,' a qualifier the statute leaves undefined, and it does not address what remedy, if any, is available to an employee for a breach of this confidentiality duty -- that is not stated in the confidentiality subdivisions themselves. It also does not independently verify whether any other statute (for example, general personnel-file or privacy statutes) supplies additional confidentiality protection. The Government Code § 12945.8(c)(3) and § 12945.8(e)(7)(D) citations below are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(d)(3) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the leave provisions above, Government Code § 12945.8(e)(1) requires an employer to provide reasonable accommodations for an employee who is a victim, or whose family member is a victim, of a qualifying act of violence, when the employee requests an accommodation for the employee's safety while at work. Unlike the additional leave purposes discussed above, this accommodation duty is not limited to employers with 25 or more employees. Section 12945.8(e)(2) gives examples of reasonable accommodations, including a transfer, reassignment, modified schedule, changed work telephone or permission to carry a telephone at work, changed work station, installed lock, assistance documenting an incident, an implemented safety procedure, another adjustment to a job structure, workplace facility, or work requirement, or referral to a victim assistance organization. Section 12945.8(f) separately makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or attempt to exercise, any right provided under the section. Former Labor Code § 230(f)(1) contained a substantively similar reasonable-accommodation duty.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(e)(1), reasonable accommodation duty (no employer-size limit stated)
citations.quote: (1) An employer shall provide reasonable accommodations for an employee who is a victim or whose family member is a victim of a qualifying act of violence who requests an accommodation for the safety of the employee while at work.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(e)(2), examples of reasonable accommodations
citations.quote: (2) For purposes of this subdivision, reasonable accommodations may include the implementation of safety measures, including a transfer, reassignment, modified schedule, changed work telephone, permission to carry telephone at work, changed work station, installed lock, assistance in documenting domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or another qualifying act of violence that occurs in the workplace, an implemented safety procedure, or another adjustment to a job structure, workplace facility, or work requirement in response to domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or other qualifying act of violence, or referral to a victim assistance organization.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(f), general anti-interference provision
citations.quote: (f) It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230(f)(1), the historical version of the same reasonable-accommodation duty
citations.quote: (1) An employer shall provide reasonable accommodations for a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, who requests an accommodation for the safety of the victim while at work.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not attempt to define 'undue hardship,' a limit on the accommodation duty that the statute defines by cross-reference to Government Code § 12926 and Labor Code § 6400, both of which this document did not independently fetch or verify. It also does not restate the accommodation-specific certification and six-month recertification provisions found in § 12945.8(e)(7), addressing only the confidentiality portion of that paragraph in a separate clause. The Government Code § 12945.8(e)(1), § 12945.8(e)(2), and § 12945.8(f) citations below are all from the same section and are not independent of one another; the Labor Code § 230(f)(1) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of all three.
